newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Formosa confirms in $3 bln China project.
newsitem.headline: Formosa confirms in $3 bln China project.

text.p: The chairman of Taiwan's Formosa Plastics Wang Yung-ching confirmed on Saturday the group had started building a US$3 billion thermal power plant in China's coastal Fujian province despite not having Taipei's approval.
"(Formosa Plastics group) has begun construction (of the China project)," Wang said on state television replying to journalists' question.

This was the first time Formosa had confirmed rumours that the group had started construction of the project. Previously, it had insisted that if the Taiwan government disagreed, it would not go ahead with the project.
"Once (the construction) started, we cannot say stop it.

"If the government approves it, we are happy to do what we originally planned to do...but if the government disapproves it, we intend to wait and see whether the government policy can be changed," Wang said.

The 82-year-old Wang, nicknamed "god of management" and one of the richest in Taiwan, completed his 5,000-metre jog in 42 minutes during the group's annual athletic meeting on Saturday, the television report said.

State television said if the government still did not approve the project, Formosa will not use funds from either its domestic member companies or its overseas affiliates, but instead may seek foreign funds.

In June 1996, the three key group members Formosa Plastics, Nan Ya Plastics and Formosa Chemical and Fiber announced plans to build the $3 billion, 3,600-megawatt Fujian plant in partnership with Fujian authorities.

The group applied for Taiwan state approval but publicly backed out two months later after Taiwan president Lee Teng-hui appealed to local enterprises to slow their investments in the arch rival Chinese mainland.

President Lee Teng-hui has argued the need to review Taiwan's policy of targeting China as a main market for fear that over-dependence on China investment could increase its political vulnerability in their half century-old rivalry.
Taiwan investment must be routed indirectly through Hong Kong or other third parties and must have Taiwan government approval.
Taiwan officials concede, however, that there is little they can do if local firms choose to route investments through overseas subsidiaires or affiliates.

Taiwan and China have been rivals since a civil war split them in 1949, with Beijing's communist government regarding the Nationalist-ruled island as a renegade province that ultimately must be reunified with the mainland.
Nearly 30,000 Taiwan firms have poured some US$30 billion into mainland China since a political thaw in the late 1980s, but the flow slowed in 1996 after political tensions and Lee's go-slow appeals.
